newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-KwaZulu-Natal says S.Africa future by the sea.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-KwaZulu-Natal says S.Africa future by the sea.

text.p: South Africa's economy was founded on the gold below its high inland plateau but on the coast they say the future is by the ocean waves.

KwaZulu-Natal, through whose ports the bulk of South African trade passes, hopes the changing face of the economy will lure foreign business to its shores and not to the industrial hub around Johannesburg and Pretoria, 600 km (360 miles) inland.

"Historically Johannesburg is where it is because of the mines. Now you will see a movement away from reliance on that area because the main reason for its existence is decreasing," said Cliff Bell, who promotes investment in KwaZulu-Natal.
"If we become more export-oriented and attract more foreign investors, you will see the coast growing at a more rapid pace."
South Africa's economy is still heavily dependent on gold, diamond and other minerals from its mines but diversification began long ago and is a key government goal.

The KwaZulu-Natal Marketing Initiative (KMI) is trying to convince foreign investors, on whom the new democratic nation is pinning so much hope now that apartheid-era sanctions have fallen, that they needn't traipse inland.
"Why should manufacturers locate their plants so many hundreds of kilometres from strategic ports?" asked the province's outgoing premier, Frank Mdlalose.
"Transport in South Africa is very expensive. It costs as much to ship a container from Durban to London as it does to send it by road from Durban to Pretoria," said the KMI's Bell.
HARD SELL AND LOCATION BENEFIT ZULU PROVINCE
Figures show KwaZulu-Natal's hard sell, capitalising on what it says is a prime location, has been a success envied by the rest of a country still awaiting the hoped-for investment boom.

With just a fifth of South Africa's 42 million people, the small province, once dependent on ubiquitous sugar and timber plantations, attracted over a third of all foreign industrial investments registered by the government from 1991 to 1996.

This is despite its notoriety as the only part of the new South Africa where political violence, between supporters of President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress and the provincially dominant Inkatha Freedom Party, is still raging.
Peace efforts have quelled the worst of the killing, which political analysts said was of little concern to business as it was not aimed at them and happened largely in distant villages.

More economically worrying is South Africa's violent crime wave, cited as a key negative factor by potential investors, but this afflicts the country as a whole and is worse in Johannesburg than Durban.
JOHANNESBURG TIES UP WITH MAPUTO

KMI, set up by the provincial authorities but with major private-sector involvement, has lured most investors from Asia, mainly Taiwan -- whose further interest is in jeopardy after President Nelson Mandela cut ties in favour of Beijing.
In the year to March 1996, KMI brought in foreign investment worth some 180 million rand ($40 million), creating 3,200 jobs in an area where one in three is unemployed.

In this financial year, the biggest deal was a 40 million rand sodium chlorate plant which a Canadian unit of Sterling Chemicals is to set up in Richards Bay, one of many areas eligible for tax holidays and other state incentives.
Bell said that increasingly, investors were setting up in South Africa not to sell to the locals but to export their goods, and that this worked in favour of the coastal cities.

Asian manufacturers, for example, get round U.S. import limits on their domestic produce by selling textiles made in South Africa, whose exports under apartheid were little welcome but which at present is not subject to quotas.

"Before the 1994 elections, industries that set up here only exported about 15 percent of their goods, as exports were blocked by sanctions. Now it's about 30 percent and nearly all foreign firms are exporting," said Bell.
"Being on the coast helps us a great deal."
PRIORITY FOR JOB-RICH MANUFACTURING

Manufacturing, given priority since it is labour-intensive, now accounts for 30 percent of KwaZulu-Natal's earnings, followed on 17 percent by commerce and tourism -- thanks to warm winters, unspoilt beaches and breathtaking mountains.
Agriculture lags behind at five percent.

The province faces stiff competition from the Johannesburg area, where industry is long-established, and from the Western Cape, which has the attractive magnet of Cape Town but is far from the population centres and trade routes of southern Africa.
Bell says only his region has the twin advantages of easy sea access and excellent rail and road links to Johannesburg and beyond.

"KwaZulu-Natal is well situated for foreign investment. It is on the eastern seaboard and has South Africa's two largest ports, Durban and Richards Bay, which together account for 70 percent of South Africa's cargo traffic," he said.

Johannesburg, hoping to decrease reliance on the two ports, is promoting a link-up with Mozambique's capital Maputo, whose port, slightly nearer, is being revived after the end of a two-decade civil war.
